claims.claim: Palpation is the physical examination technique of using the hands to feel the body for abnormalities; the OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing text (section 12.3) describes it as assessing the texture, temperature, moisture, and size of organs and tissues.
Palpation gathers information that inspection alone cannot provide, which is why the two techniques work as a pair: look first, then touch.

In the standard physical exam sequence, inspection is typically the first step and palpation follows; the abdomen is the documented special case where auscultation of bowel sounds precedes palpation so the sounds are heard undisturbed.

Light palpation uses gentle pressure — about 0.5 inch (roughly 1 cm) of indentation in abdominal work — to assess surface characteristics such as musculature, superficial masses, and tenderness; deep palpation presses further to assess organs and internal structures and is typically performed by advanced practice clinicians.

Palpation can reveal texture, temperature, moisture, tenderness, masses, and pulses; for example, pulses are felt where arteries run close to the surface, and palpation of peripheral pulses provides heart rate, rhythm, and strength.
When a patient reports pain, the clinician palpates the tender area last, and the patient's response during palpation — verbal reports, wincing, guarding, or rigidity — is itself assessment data.

Comfort practice is part of technique: cold hands and a cold room make patients tense (voluntary guarding), so clinicians warm their hands and the room and move gently to keep the patient relaxed during palpation.
Palpation findings are objective data recorded in the chart; a documented entry such as 'skin warm and dry' is a palpation finding written down.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Order of the exam techniques: general sequence lists palpation immediately after inspection, but the abdominal assessment places auscultation before palpation.
positions: General body systems: inspection first, then palpation (OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing 12.3).
Abdomen: auscultation precedes palpation so bowel sounds are not disturbed by touch (OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills 27.2).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Teach the general look-first-then-touch sequence as the rule, and mention the abdominal exception in one clause, noting that its full treatment belongs to the auscultation and percussion lessons. No contradiction is asserted between the two texts; both are presented with their context.

sourceRecords.notes: Reused existing registry id (identical URL). Read 2026-08-22 via the Medicine LibreTexts mirror of section 27.2 'Physical Assessment' (abdomen chapter). Supports: palpation as touching with the flat of the hand and fingers to detect organs, masses, and tenderness; palpating a painful area last; light palpation at about 0.5 in (~1 cm) of pressure beginning in the RLQ; deep palpation by advanced practice clinicians to assess enlarged organs; noting the patient's response (pain, guarding, rigidity); voluntary guarding from fear, anxiety, or the touch of cold hands; warming the room and stethoscope to reduce patient tensing; and the abdominal order exception (auscultation before palpation). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
